name: Echo

question.stem: A 2-year-old girl presents to the clinic for follow-up after having an abnormal echocardiogram, which was obtained due to her mother’s history of bicuspid aortic valve. The echocardiogram revealed a normal aortic valve and an incidental finding of a patent foramen ovale. She has no other significant past medical history.
question.prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Antiplatelet therapy after 5 years of age
Device closure after 5 years of age

explanation.text: Patent foramen ovale (PFO) is a common finding in the general population, with persistence in approximately 20%-25% of individuals beyond early childhood. In most cases, PFO represents a normal variant of atrial septal anatomy rather than a pathologic condition. In this asymptomatic and otherwise healthy patient, no intervention is necessary. The risk of ischemic stroke in pediatric patients with an incidental finding of PFO is extremely low, and routine closure or medical therapy is not indicated. Intervention usually is recommended in older patients with ischemic stroke who are subsequently found to have a PFO. In that situation, the stroke is assumed to have been caused by a paradoxical embolism, due to transient right-to-left shunting through the PFO. Even in pediatric patients with stroke, the role of PFO treatment is controversial.

In an adult patient found to have a PFO after experiencing a cryptogenic stroke, device closure now would be appropriate. Pediatric data are limited and do not support routine closure, in particular when there is no history of stroke.

There is no reason for this patient to undergo device closure after 5 years of age if the PFO has not closed spontaneously by then; age alone is not an indication for closure. Even in older children or adults, closure is only considered in specific high-risk scenarios, such as recurrent cryptogenic stroke attributed to the PFO.

Antiplatelet therapy now is not appropriate because there is no evidence supporting this treatment in asymptomatic patients with an incidental PFO. Medical therapy is typically reserved for patients with a history of thromboembolic events, such as ischemic stroke, in whom the PFO may be contributory.

Antiplatelet therapy after 5 years of age, even if the PFO remains open, is not appropriate without any history of stroke or risk for thromboembolism. Antiplatelet therapy is reserved for patients with a history of thromboembolic events or other vascular risk factors.

testingPoint: Know that an incidental finding of a patent foramen ovale (PFO) in an asymptomatic child requires no intervention, as the risk for ischemic stroke is very low.
